GS Paper III · Economy · Chapter 7 of 8

Investment and Infrastructure: PPP, NIP, NMP, Gati Shakti, LogisticsPriority: see PYQ box

Handout pp 108-120Handwritten format · mnemonics and PYQs at each topic2022 (PPP / infrastructure)
PRIORITY: HIGH for Mains (PPP and infrastructure appear almost every alternate year, 2013-2022)PYQ years: 2013 PPP pros and cons · 2014 PPP liabilities · 2017 airports PPP · 2020 concession agreement · 2022 PPP railway stations
THIS CHAPTER IN 60 SECONDS
  • Infrastructure financing is not only money: it is bankability, project preparation, risk allocation and investor confidence. Tools: PPP, NIP, NMP, PM Gati Shakti.
  • PPP = private capital + public purpose + long-term service delivery. India had 4 phases; over 1,200 projects worth ₹7.2 lakh crore; 11 PPP models (BOT-Toll, BOT-Annuity, BOO, BOOT, EPC, HAM, DBFO, BOLT, LDO, ROT, DBO, TOT).
  • Kelkar Committee (revitalising PPPs) gives a five-box fix: external factors, legal and regulatory, financing, governance, contractual design.
  • NIP: ₹111 lakh crore investment, FY2020-25 (Atanu Chakraborty Task Force). NMP: ₹10 lakh crore of assets to be monetised in the next 5 years (Budget 2025-26); no privatisation, assets return.
  • PM Gati Shakti (2021): from fragmented project planning to system-level infrastructure planning; National Logistics Policy (Sept 2022): logistics cost 7.97% of GDP (FY24).
Understand it firstThink of a city building a new bridge. The government may lack the money or the speed, so it invites a private builder (PPP). To plan which bridges, it keeps a list (NIP); to raise money without selling the land it leases old bridges (NMP); to avoid every department digging its own trench, it keeps one common map (Gati Shakti). This picture is a memory aid, not from the handout.
WORDS YOU NEED FIRST
WordPlain meaning (aid: verify before quoting)
Brownfield / greenfieldBrownfield: an already built asset being upgraded or leased. Greenfield: a brand-new project.
ConcessionRight given to a private party to run a public asset for a period.
Viability Gap Funding (VGF)Grant that makes an economically useful but commercially weak project bankable.
Swiss ChallengeA private party offers an unsolicited proposal; others get a chance to beat it.
Obsolescing bargainThe private player loses bargaining power over time after it has sunk its money.
Risk allocation principleGive each risk to the party best able to manage it.
MonetisationRaising money from an existing asset without selling it permanently.
REIT / InvITTrusts that pool investor money to own income-earning real estate / infrastructure.
MultimodalUsing road, rail, ports, air and waterways together as one system.
RememberOne line to carry: PPP is a trust-based, transparent, technology-driven partnership balancing fiscal responsibility with service excellence (the teacher's conclusion on p.114).

1 · INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCING
PYQ 2020 · 15m · investment as capital formation; concession agreement design (your file)Handout p.108 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstA road or port needs money now and pays back over decades. India mixes public capex, private capital, institutional finance and asset recycling. The teacher's point: the problem is not only the amount, but whether projects are bankable, well prepared and fairly risk-shared. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Infrastructure financing = mobilisation of public capex + private capital + institutional finance + asset recycling.
  • The financing challenge is not only money but also bankability, project preparation, risk allocation and investor confidence.
Data and trends (teacher)
  • Shift from bank-credit dependence to alternate financing and capital market instruments.
  • Bank credit growth 4.5% in October 2025 (YoY).
  • NBFC credit flow to the commercial sector, FY20 to FY25: 43.3% CAGR.
  • Non-food bank credit, FY20 to FY25: 25% CAGR.
  • REITs / InvITs enable long-term institutional capital.

2 · PUBLIC PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP (PPP)
PYQ 2013 · 10m · PPP pros and consPYQ 2014 · 12.5m · PPP and liabilities passed to the futurePYQ 2017 · 10m · airports through JV under PPPPYQ 2022 · 10m · need for PPP, railway stations redevelopmentHandout pp.109-114
Understand it firstPPP is a contract between a public body and a private company: the company brings money and skill, the public body keeps the purpose (a service for citizens), and the risks are divided in writing. Success depends on who bears which risk. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • PPP → mechanism for private capital + public purpose + long-term service delivery.
  • A mechanism that allows the government to procure and implement public infrastructure or service using the resources and expertise of the private sector (World Bank).
  • Teacher's flow: public capital → increasing private participation → capacity building and confidence-building measures. Contract between a government entity and private companies → clearly defined risk sharing.
Need of PPP in India
Four needs (teacher)
1 Addressing infrastructural bottlenecks that constrain growth and job creation
2 Public investment alone is insufficient due to fiscal constraints
3 PPP brings private capital, managerial efficiency and innovation (e.g. Delhi airport: GMR managed)
4 PPP attracts domestic and global institutional funds
  • 5 Contracts link payments to performance and service quality, ensuring accountability (e.g. Mundra Port (Adani Group): faster turnaround).
  • 6 Enables optimal risk sharing and reduces uncertainty (e.g. HAM highway projects).
  • 7 Shifts focus from asset creation to service delivery.
Evolution of PPP models in India (teacher)
PhaseDetail
Phase 1: early 2000s emergencePolicy reform encouraged private participation · India emerged as a leading PPP market globally · focus on conventional BOT models
Phase 2: institutional development (2006 onwards)Creation of PPP Appraisal Committee · introduction of Viability Gap Funding · development of standard contracts
Phase 3: market maturity and recognitionOver 1,200 PPP projects worth ₹7.2 lakh crore implemented · global recognition: 1st in operational maturity (Infrascope 2015)
Phase 4: PPP 2.0 (current reform phase)Focus on revitalisation and restructuring · introduction of Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) · launch of National Monetisation Pipeline

Types of PPP models (handout table, p.110)
ModelHow it worksExample
Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT-Toll)Private sector finances, builds and operates the asset for a fixed concession period. Revenue from tolls / user charges. Traffic risk borne by the private player.Delhi-Gurugram Expressway
BOT-AnnuityPrivate sector builds and operates; government pays a fixed annuity. Demand / traffic risk borne by the government.National Highway projects under NHAI
Build-Own-Operate (BOO)Private sector builds, owns and operates the asset permanently; revenue from sale of services.Independent Power Producers
Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT)Private ownership during the concession; asset transferred to government later; revenue from facility operations.Power and port projects
Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC)Government finances the project fully; private player designs, constructs and hands over. Major risks borne by government.Bharatmala highway stretches
Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM)Government pays 40% during construction; private sector bears 60%, recovered through annuity after completion. Traffic risk borne by government.NH projects under Bharatmala
Design-Build-Finance-Operate (DBFO)Private sector designs, finances, builds and operates; revenue through user charges or annuity.Highway PPP projects
Build-Own-Lease-Transfer (BOLT)Private party builds and owns the asset, leases it to the government, transfers later; revenue through lease rentals.Railway infrastructure projects
Lease-Develop-Operate (LDO)Existing public asset leased to a private operator for development and operation; ownership remains with government.Airport modernisation projects
Rehabilitate-Operate-Transfer (ROT)Existing infrastructure upgraded, operated and later transferred back; revenue from operations during the concession.Port terminals, road upgradation
Design-Build-Operate (DBO)Private sector designs, builds and operates; financing largely public; operational risk with private party.Water and wastewater treatment plants
Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT)Existing operational public asset monetised; private player pays an upfront fee, operates and collects tolls.NHAI TOT bundles
Benefits of using PPP models (five stakeholders)
StakeholderBenefits (teacher, p.111)
1 GovernmentAccelerated infrastructure creation: faster execution without stretching fiscal capacity · fiscal prudence: mobilising private capital reduces pressure on public expenditure · outcome orientation: focus on policy design and regulation rather than execution · improved transparency and accountability
2 Private sectorReduced risk exposure (e.g. HAM) · business opportunities and predictable returns · enhanced efficiency and innovation (e.g. performance-linked payments) · reduced bureaucratic delays and implementation bottlenecks
3 Financial intermediaries and investorsNew investment channels: long-term, low-risk projects suitable for banks, insurance and pension funds
4 Citizens and societyBetter service delivery and improved reliability · affordable services (long-term financing and efficiency gains reduce user costs) · stimulates job creation and economic growth · public trust: confidence in governance
5 Overall economyBridging the infrastructure gap · boosting economic growth · improved investment climate that attracts global capital and enhances investor confidence
MNEMONICGreat Projects Invite Citizens' EconomyGovernment · Private sector · Investors and intermediaries · Citizens and society · Economy: the five stakeholders in the teacher's order. (own memory aid)

Issues and challenges associated with PPP versus the Kelkar Committee fix (p.112)
AreaIssues and challenges (teacher)V. Kelkar Committee recommendations
1 External factors1.1 Global economic slowdown and credit crisis (e.g. 2008 subprime crisis) · 1.2 Judicial and statutory order (e.g. mining ban in Goa delayed PPP projects)1.1 Set up an Infrastructure PPP Adjudication Tribunal for fast-track resolution · 1.2 Standardise force majeure clause to handle macro shocks
2 Legal and regulatory framework2.1 Lack of independent regulator · 2.2 Slow dispute resolution · 2.3 Unsolicited Swiss Challenge proposals2.1 Make a National PPP Policy · 2.2 Establish domain-specific independent regulators · 2.3 Use competitive and transparent procurement and bidding
3 Financing and funding issues3.1 Intergenerational liability shifting creating fiscal burden for the future · 3.2 Lack of refinancing and debt market · 3.3 DCCO-linked asset classification norms turned PPP loans into NPAs (e.g. BOT faced financial stress; HAM introduced to address this)3.1 Encourage refinance, zero-coupon bonds to avoid front-loading tariffs · 3.2 Asset monetisation of stable brownfield assets · 3.3 Successful infrastructure projects may be divested by offering to long-term investors
4 Governance / institutional issues4.1 Ministries, ULBs, line agencies lack trained personnel · 4.2 Multiplicity of agencies · 4.3 Lack of protection for officers discourages proactive measures4.1 Create a national centre of excellence for PPPs · 4.2 Amend the Prevention of Corruption Act to distinguish bona fide errors from mala fide acts · 4.3 Strengthen PPP cells in ministries via capacity building
5 Contractual framework and design flaws5.1 Risk not assigned to the entity best equipped to manage it · 5.2 One-size-fits-all approach · 5.3 Design flaws in contracts5.1 Build clear triggers, process and benchmark for renegotiation (the page ends here)
MNEMONICEvery Lender Fears Great ContractsExternal factors · Legal and regulatory · Financing and funding · Governance / institutional · Contractual and design flaws: the five boxes for both issues and Kelkar fixes. (own memory aid)

Measures taken for PPP (teacher, p.113)
  • Public Private Partnership Appraisal Committee for appraisal and approval of central-sector PPP projects.
  • India Infrastructure Project Development Fund for transaction advisory and bankable project preparation.
  • Three-year PPP project pipeline for investor visibility.
  • Standardised documents: Model Request for Qualification, Model Request for Proposal and Model Concession Agreements.
  • Waterfall framework for choosing the appropriate project implementation mode.
  • Capacity-building programme for states, Union Territories and ministries.
  • National Infrastructure Enablement Index to assess institutional preparedness.
Viability Gap Funding scheme for PPP (handout infographic)
What is it?Government financial support for PPP projects that are economically desirable but commercially unviable; a Central Sector Scheme
Funding supportUp to 40% of total project cost: 20% by Central Government + 20% by State / statutory authority
PurposeMakes weak-revenue projects bankable and attracts private investment
Sectors eligibleRoads, ports, water supply, wastewater, solid waste, health, education and other infrastructure
Way forward for PPP (teacher)
  • Strengthen the third "P": Partnership.
  • Expand scope of PPP: healthcare, social services, urban transport, railways and warehousing.
  • Legal and policy reforms: reform the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 to distinguish bona fide error from corrupt practice; remove Swiss Challenge model concerns.
  • Create a PPP Institute of Excellence.
  • Use clear communication to present PPP as service partnership, not asset sale.
  • Improve greenfield project financing: partial credit guarantees, take-out financing and standardised refinancing.
  • Long-term capital: REITs / InvITs, Alternate Investment Funds, pension funds and insurance funds.

3 · NATIONAL INFRASTRUCTURE PIPELINE (NIP)
Handout p.115 (teacher's handwriting + infographic)
Understand it firstThe NIP is the government's shopping list of infrastructure projects for five years, with an estimate of how much money is needed and where it can come from. Memory aid, not from the handout.
Atanu Chakraborty Task Force Report (terms of reference)
Identify technically feasible and financially viable infrastructure projects for FY 2020-2025
Estimate annual infrastructure investment / capital costs
Guide ministries to identify sources of financing
Suggest measures for project monitoring
  • Recommendation: ₹111 lakh crore of investment (2020-2025).
Constituents of NIP (infographic)Detail
Economic and social infrastructure projectsas per the Harmonised Master List of Infrastructure
Greenfield under constructionprojects ≥ ₹100 crore per project
Brownfielddevelopment of completed projects
Projects under conceptualisationpipeline additions
→ NIPall of the above
Benefits of NIP by stakeholder (infographic)Detail
Economywell-planned NIP enables more infrastructure projects, creates jobs, improves ease of living and gives equitable access, making growth more inclusive
Governmentenhances economic activity, creates additional fiscal space by improving the revenue base, ensures quality of expenditure focused on productive areas
Developersbetter-prepared projects, reduced aggressive bids / failure in delivery, enhanced access to finance from higher investor confidence
Banks / financial institutions / investorsinvestor confidence as projects are better prepared, exposures less likely to suffer stress given active monitoring

4 · NATIONAL MONETISATION PIPELINE (NMP)
Handout p.116 (teacher's handwriting + NITI Aayog figures)
Understand it firstNMP leases finished government assets (roads, rail, power lines) to private operators for a fixed time and earns money; the asset comes back to the government after the period. Memory aid, not from the handout.
Asset monetisation structure (NITI Aayog figure, p.116)
Public authority → concession → private investor(s)
Private investor(s) → consideration → public authority
Asset / rights, operations and maintenance by the private investor
  • No privatisation: assets are returned after the period (teacher, in red).
Objectives of NMP (NITI Aayog)Detail
Scale of financingbrings out clearly the scale of financing through asset monetisation
Phasingof the proposed monetisation and capital generated over the medium term
Guidanceon asset / project profile and method of monetisation
Operational contoursof the project / asset (lane-km of road, circuit km, etc.)
Asset monetisation cycle (handout figure)
Existing asset base → monetise existing assets → proceeds from monetisation → new infrastructure creation → (back to the existing asset base)
Benefits (teacher)Challenges (teacher)
Unlocks the value of existing assets → lower O&M cost to governmentEnhanced role of government for asset creation
Raises finance without ownership lossFinancing: REITs / InvITs, low awareness
Risk-averse private sector → government creates assetsPeople: high user charges
Better O&M through user charges, not taxpayers' moneyGlobal economic slowdown; lack of an independent regulatory authority in the sector (→ PPP agreements, user charges, disputes)

5 · PM GATI SHAKTI
PYQ 2021 · 15m · infrastructure for inclusive growth (Chapter 5)Handout pp.117-119 (teacher's handwriting)
Understand it firstBefore Gati Shakti every department planned its own road, pipe or rail line, often digging the same ground twice. Gati Shakti puts all plans on one digital map (a GIS platform) so projects are sequenced together. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Umbrella initiative for integrated multimodal infrastructure planning, launched in 2021.
  • National Master Plan → GIS-based digital platform under PM Gati Shakti.
  • Driven by 7 engines: roads, railways, airports, ports, mass transport, waterways, logistics infrastructure.
Core shift (teacher's red box)
Fromfragmented project planning
Tosystem-level infrastructure planning
Progress
  • 57 ministries / departments onboarded.
  • District Master Plan → 28 Aspirational Districts covered, to be extended to 112 districts.
  • Over 1,700 data layers integrated into the National Master Plan.
  • 27 States notified State Logistics Policies.
Current issues
  • Departmental silos and poor inter-ministerial coordination.
  • Fragmented planning across Centre, State and private sector.
  • Time and cost overruns in infrastructure projects.
  • Weak last-mile connectivity.
  • Multiple clearances, NOC delays.
  • Poor integration of roads, railways, ports and industrial corridors.
  • Limited use of real-time data in project planning.
Features of the programme
  • GIS-based National Master Plan; multimodal connectivity planning; schemes integrated: Sagarmala, Bharatmala, UDAN, Inland Waterways, Dry / land ports (teacher's star).
  • Corridors included: industrial corridors, defence corridors, manufacturing and fishing clusters, social infrastructure mapping.
  • Gati Shakti Sanchar Portal: centralised Right of Way (RoW) approvals; faster rollout of telecom infrastructure.
  • District Master Plan Portal; PM Gati Shakti public datasets; Standard Operating Procedures for data accuracy.
  • PM Gati Shakti Public and Unified Geospatial Interface: gives private users curated data sets.

6 · NATIONAL LOGISTICS POLICY
Handout p.120 (typed)
Understand it firstLogistics cost is the money spent moving and storing goods. When it falls, every Indian product becomes cheaper to sell at home and abroad. The Policy sets a clear target: top 25 on the Logistics Performance Index by 2030. Memory aid, not from the handout.
  • Launched 17 September 2022. Objective: an integrated, efficient and cost-effective logistics network. Aim: India among the top 25 countries on the Logistics Performance Index by 2030. Promotes data-driven decision-making.
Data / progressFigure
Logistics cost8.79% of GDP (FY22), 8.84% (FY23) → 7.97% (FY24)
State Logistics Policies27 States notified
ULIP (Unified Logistics Interface Platform)connects 44 systems across 11 ministries
Companies on ULIPmore than 1,700
Challenges
  • Reduce logistics cost further.
  • Improve India's LPI ranking.
  • Wider State-level alignment through State Logistics Policies.
  • Stronger digital integration across logistics systems.
  • Better EXIM cargo tracking and visibility.
  • Sector-specific logistics planning, e.g. cement.
Measures taken
  • State Logistics Policies notified by States; ULIP connects systems across ministries.
  • LEADS (Logistics Ease Across Different States) reports assess logistics performance; the 6th LEADS report (January 2024) introduced "Sustainable Logistics" as a new pillar.
  • Logistics Data Bank tracks containerised EXIM cargo using RFID, IoT, Big Data and cloud.
  • Sectoral Plan for Efficient Logistics for the cement industry (multimodal connectivity and digital transparency).
Way forward
  • Deepen digital logistics integration: expand ULIP for real-time data, cargo visibility, inter-ministerial coordination.
  • Use LEADS for targeted state reforms: convert benchmarking into reforms in infrastructure, services and regulation.
  • Prepare sector-specific logistics plans: replicate the cement plan for other bulk sectors.
  • Percolate planning to districts through District Master Plan modules.
  • Reduce logistics friction for GVCs: predictability, lower cost, manufacturing and export competitiveness.

TRAPS AND EXAM-HALL RULES
TrapWhy it fools youExam-hall rule
HAM split.Government pays 40% during construction; private bears 60% (recovered through annuity); traffic risk is the government's.Write the split with who bears traffic risk.
BOT-Toll versus BOT-Annuity.Toll: private bears traffic risk. Annuity: government bears demand / traffic risk.Add the risk bearer each time.
NMP is privatisation.The teacher stresses no privatisation: assets are returned after the period.Write "lease / concession, asset returns".
NIP versus NMP.NIP = list of projects to be built (₹111 lakh crore). NMP = assets to be leased out (₹10 lakh crore).Say "build list" and "lease list".
VGF share.Up to 40%: 20% Centre + 20% State / statutory authority.Write the 20 + 20.
Kelkar column ends at 5.1.The page shows no recommendation text for 5.2 and 5.3.Do not invent the missing points.

  • Q1. Under HAM the government pays during construction: (a) 20% (b) 40% (c) 60% (d) 100%

  • Q4. VGF total maximum share of project cost: (a) 20% (b) 30% (c) 40% (d) 50%

ABBREVIATION COLUMN
Abbreviation columnEvery short form in this chapter, with its full form and a one-line plain meaning. The meanings are plain-language aids to help revision: verify them before quoting in an answer.

BOLT: Build-Own-Lease-Transfer. private builds, leases to government, then transfers

BOO: Build-Own-Operate. private builds, owns and operates permanently

BOOT: Build-Own-Operate-Transfer. asset passes to government after concession

BOT: Build-Operate-Transfer. private builds and runs for a concession, then transfers

CAGR: Compound Annual Growth Rate. smoothed yearly growth rate

DBFO: Design-Build-Finance-Operate. private does all four; paid by user charges or annuity

DBO: Design-Build-Operate. public finance, private builds and operates

DP: DP World. private partner in NSICT

DPR: Detailed Project Report. project plan used for approval

EPC: Engineering, Procurement and Construction. government funds fully; private builds

ES: Economic Survey.

EXIM: Export-Import.

FY: Financial Year. April to March accounting year (FY25 = 2024-25)

FY20: Financial Year 2019-20.

FY2024: Financial Year 2024. the year used for the logistics-cost estimate

FY21: Financial Year 2020-21.

FY22: Financial Year 2021-22.

FY23: Financial Year 2022-23. April 2022 to March 2023

FY24: Financial Year 2023-24. year of earlier ODI figure

FY25: Financial Year 2024-25. April 2024 to March 2025

GDP: Gross Domestic Product. value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year

GFCF: Gross Fixed Capital Formation. investment in assets like machinery, buildings and infrastructure; the investment part of GDP

GIS: Geographic Information System. digital map layers used by Gati Shakti

GMR: GMR Group. operator of Delhi airport (teacher example)

GW: Gigawatt.

HAM: Hybrid Annuity Model. govt 40% in construction, private 60% via annuity

IAS: Indian Administrative Service.

IoT: Internet of Things. everyday devices connected to the internet (a future-skills ITI course)

JNPT: Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust. public partner in NSICT

LDO: Lease-Develop-Operate. existing public asset leased for development

LEADS: Logistics Ease Across Different States. state logistics performance report

LPI: Logistics Performance Index. World Bank ranking of logistics quality

NBFC: Non-Banking Financial Company. lender that is not a bank

NH: National Highway.

NHAI: National Highways Authority of India. builds and manages national highways

NIP: National Infrastructure Pipeline. ₹111 lakh crore project list for FY2020-25

NITI: National Institution for Transforming India. government think tank (NITI Aayog)

NLP: National Logistics Policy. launched 17 Sep 2022

NMP: National Monetisation Pipeline. leasing existing public assets to raise money; asset returns

NOC: No Objection Certificate. permission needed from an agency

NSICT: Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal. first private container terminal (JNPT with DP World, BOT)

OCR: Optical Character Recognition. text layer read from page images; can be garbled

PM: Prime Minister. head of the Union government

PPP: Public-Private Partnership. project shared between government and private firm

PVTG: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group.

REIT: Real Estate Investment Trust. pooled investor money in income-earning property

RFID: Radio Frequency Identification. tag used for cargo tracking

RFP: Request for Proposal. bidding document

RFQ: Request for Quote. electronic platform for bond trades

ROT: Rehabilitate-Operate-Transfer. upgrade existing asset, operate, hand back

TOT: Toll-Operate-Transfer. upfront fee for an existing operating asset

UDAN: Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik. regional air connectivity scheme

ULIP: Unified Logistics Interface Platform. links logistics systems across ministries

VGF: Viability Gap Funding. government grant that makes a project financially workable
